newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe inflation seen rising into third-quarter.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe inflation seen rising into third-quarter.

text.p: Stubbornly high money supply growth and slightly higher food prices due to reduced harvest forecasts are likely to keep Zimbabwe inflation on an upward trend until September, economic analysts said on Thursday.

The state Central Statistical Office (CSO) said the southern African country's all-items consumer price index rose 2.6 percentage points in March from February, lifting the year-on-year inflation rate to 19.9 percent.
The figure was consistent with the central Reserve Bank forecasts that annual inflation would remain within a 19 to 21 percent range until mid-year.

"The inflation figure for March is pretty well within our expectations and confirms our forecasts that inflation will be on an upward trend for the foreseeable future," said capital markets analyst Jason Moore of economic analysts Dataworld.
Danny Dube, chairman of the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce's economic committee, said the upward track in inflation was largely technical coming off from a low base last year.
He said some bread and staple maize-meal price increases earlier this year were only factored in in March, also contributing to the higher figure.
"But there's no reason to expect that inflation will come down in the short to medium term," Dube told Reuters.

"This year we see inflation caused by food price increases is likely to be higher again because harvests have been affected by the rains," he said referring to press reports on Thursday that Zimbabwe was likely to produce just over two million tonnes of the staple maize crop, down from forecasts of 2.6 million tonnes.
Agriculture officials were unavaible for comment on the reports but last March they warned of crop damage due to waterlogging and disease.
Dube said food prices still weighed heavily on the inflation basket and that any slight movement there impacted heavily on the overall inflation figure.

He and Moore said non-food inflation, particularly the country's high money supply growth, which has averaged 28.5 percent annually since 1990, and hikes in import duties could also stoke annual inflation.

"The Reserve Bank is struggling to contain money supply growth which remains stubbornly high. There's nothing to support that inflation will come down. It will probably start doing so towards the end of the third-quarter," he said.

A stock broker said market players were becoming concerned at the "strong underlying inflationary pressures", adding that if the inflation rate continued on an upward trend, investors might start deserting equities in anticipation of better gains on the money market.
